p.src: Now Cao Pi, seeing the two women weeping, drew his sword to kill them. Suddenly a crimson radiance filled his eyes; he lowered his sword and asked, “Who are you?” One woman replied, “I am Lady Liu, wife of General Yuan.” Pi asked, “Who is this young woman?” Lady Liu replied, “She is Lady Zhen, wife of my second son, Yuan Xi. When Xi departed to govern Youzhou, Lady Zhen was unwilling to make the long journey, and so remained here.”

p.src: Pi dragged the young woman closer and saw that her hair was disheveled and her face begrimed. He wiped her face with his sleeve and looked upon her: Lady Zhen had skin like jade and features like a flower, with beauty enough to topple a kingdom. He then said to Lady Liu, “I am the son of Chancellor Cao. I shall protect your household; do not be afraid.” Then he sat in the hall with his hand upon his sword.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Cao led his generals into the city of Jizhou. As he was about to pass through the gate, Xu You spurred his horse forward, pointed at the gate with his whip, and called to Cao Cao, “A-Man, without me, how could you ever have entered this gate?” Cao Cao laughed heartily. When the generals heard this, they were all indignant. When Cao Cao reached the gate of Yuan Shao’s residence, he asked, “Who has already entered here?” The guard replied, “The heir is inside.” Cao Cao summoned him out and rebuked him. Lady Liu came out, bowed, and said, “Without the heir, my household could not have been preserved. I beg to offer Lady Zhen to serve him as his wife.” Cao Cao ordered Lady Zhen to be summoned, and she bowed before him. Looking at her, Cao Cao said, “She is indeed fit to be my son’s wife!” He then ordered Cao Pi to take her as his wife.

p.src: After pacifying Jizhou, Cao Cao personally went to Yuan Shao’s grave and made offerings. He bowed twice and wept bitterly, then turned to his generals and said, “Long ago, when Benchu and I first raised armies together, he asked me, ‘If our cause should fail, what region could we rely upon?’ I asked him, ‘And what do you intend?’ Benchu replied, ‘I shall hold the Yellow River to the south, bar my northern frontier with Yan and Dai, gather the peoples of the desert, and then turn south to contend for the realm. Might that not bring success?’ I answered, ‘I shall employ the wisdom and strength of all beneath Heaven and govern them by the proper Way; then nothing will be beyond attainment.’ Those words seem spoken only yesterday, yet now Benchu is dead. I cannot help but shed tears for him!” All present sighed with sorrow. Cao Cao bestowed gold, silks, grain, and rice upon Yuan Shao’s wife, Lady Liu. He then issued an order: “The people of Hebei have suffered the calamities of war; all their taxes and levies for this year are remitted.” At the same time, he wrote a memorial reporting matters to the imperial court; and Cao Cao himself assumed the governorship of Jizhou.

p.src: One day, Xu Chu rode through the eastern gate and happened to meet Xu You. Xu You called out to him, “Without me, how could any of you pass in and out of this gate?” Xu Chu angrily replied, “We passed through countless perils and fought bloody battles at the risk of our lives to capture this city. How dare you boast so!” Xu You cursed him, saying, “You are all mere common brutes, not worth speaking of!” Xu Chu flew into a rage, drew his sword, and killed Xu You. Carrying the severed head to Cao Cao, he said that Xu You had behaved with such insolence that he had killed him. Cao Cao said, “Ziyuan and I were old friends; he was only jesting with me. Why did you kill him?” He sternly rebuked Xu Chu and ordered that Xu You be buried with full honors. He then sent men throughout Jizhou to seek worthy scholars. The people of Jizhou said, “The Commandant of Cavalry, Cui Yan, courtesy name Jigui, is a native of Dongwucheng in Qinghe. He repeatedly offered counsel to Yuan Shao, but Yuan Shao would not heed him; therefore he feigned illness and remained at home.”

p.src: Cao Cao immediately summoned Cui Yan and appointed him administrative aide of the province, saying to him, “Yesterday I examined this province’s household registers. They record a total population of three hundred thousand; this may indeed be called a great province.” Cui Yan replied, “Today the realm has collapsed into division and the Nine Provinces are torn asunder. The two Yuan brothers contend with one another, while the bones of Jizhou’s people lie exposed across the fields. Yet instead of hastening to inquire into local conditions and rescuing the people from their misery, my lord first counts and compares the household registers. Is this what the men and women of this province hoped for from your enlightened lordship?”

p.src: Hearing this, Cao Cao’s expression changed; he thanked Cui Yan for the rebuke and treated him as an honored guest. Having secured Jizhou, Cao Cao sent men to learn news of Yuan Tan. At that time Yuan Tan was leading troops in plundering Ganling, Anping, Bohai, Hejian, and other districts. When he heard that Yuan Shang had been defeated and fled to Zhongshan, he led his army against him. Yuan Shang had no heart for battle and fled straight to Youzhou to seek refuge with Yuan Xi. Yuan Tan accepted the surrender of all Yuan Shang’s troops and planned to retake Jizhou. Cao Cao sent a man to summon him, but Yuan Tan did not come. Cao Cao was enraged. He sent a letter breaking off their marriage alliance, personally led his great army against Yuan Tan, and advanced directly to Pingyuan.

p.src: When Yuan Tan learned that Cao Cao was personally leading an army against him, he sent a messenger to Liu Biao requesting aid. Liu Biao invited Xuande to discuss the matter. Xuande said, “Cao Cao has now taken Jizhou, and the might of his army is at its height. Before long, both Yuan brothers will surely be captured by him, so aiding them would achieve nothing. Moreover, Cao Cao has long harbored designs upon Jingzhou and Xiangyang. We should merely train our troops and defend ourselves; we must not act rashly.” Liu Biao asked, “Then how should I decline his request?” Xuande replied, “You may write to the Yuan brothers, proposing reconciliation between them, and decline in courteous terms.”

p.src: When Yuan Tan received Liu Biao’s letter, he understood that Liu Biao had no intention of sending troops; he also judged that he could not withstand Cao Cao; and so he abandoned Pingyuan and fled to defend Nanpi. Cao Cao pursued him to Nanpi. The weather was bitterly cold, and all the waterways had frozen, so the grain boats could not move. Cao Cao ordered the local people to break the ice and haul the boats, but when they heard the order, they fled. Cao Cao was furious and intended to arrest and execute them. When the people heard of this, they went in person to the camp and surrendered themselves. Cao Cao said, “If I do not kill you, my commands will carry no force; yet if I kill you, I cannot bear it. Go quickly and hide in the mountains; do not let my soldiers capture you.” The people all departed in tears.

p.src: Yuan Tan led his troops out of the city to confront Cao Cao’s army. When the two armies had drawn up opposite one another, Cao Cao rode forth, pointed his whip at Yuan Tan, and cursed him: “I treated you generously; why did you turn against me?” Yuan Tan replied, “You invaded my lands, seized my cities, and even took my wife and children; yet you accuse me of disloyalty?” Cao Cao was enraged and sent Xu Huang forth. Yuan Tan sent Peng An to meet him in combat. Their horses met, and within a few bouts Xu Huang struck Peng An down from his horse. Yuan Tan’s army was defeated and fled back into Nanpi. Cao Cao sent troops to surround the city on all four sides. Alarmed, Yuan Tan sent Xin Ping to Cao Cao to negotiate surrender. Cao Cao said, “That whelp Yuan Tan is fickle and untrustworthy; I can scarcely put faith in him. I have already entrusted your younger brother, Xin Pi, with important duties. You too may remain here.” Xin Ping replied, “Chancellor, you are mistaken. I have heard it said that when the lord is honored, his ministers share his glory, and when the lord suffers, his ministers share his shame. I have served the Yuan house for many years; how could I betray it?”

p.src: Cao Cao understood that Xin Ping could not be persuaded to remain, and so sent him back. Xin Ping returned to Yuan Tan and reported that Cao Cao would not accept the surrender. Yuan Tan rebuked him: “Your younger brother now serves Cao Cao. Do you too harbor divided loyalties?” Hearing this, Xin Ping’s breast swelled with rage, and he fell unconscious to the ground. Yuan Tan ordered that he be carried out, and before long he died. Yuan Tan regretted his words. Guo Tu said to Yuan Tan, “Tomorrow drive all the common people before us, follow behind them with the army, and fight Cao Cao to the death.”

p.src: Yuan Tan followed his counsel. That night, he drove out all the people of Nanpi and made them take up swords and spears to await his orders. At daybreak the next morning, all four gates were thrown open. With the army driving them from behind, the people surged out in front amid a tremendous roar and advanced straight upon Cao Cao’s camp. The two armies fought in a confused melee from the hour of the dragon until noon. Neither side gained the advantage, and corpses covered the ground. Seeing that complete victory had not yet been won, Cao Cao rode up a hill and personally beat the war drum. When the officers and soldiers saw him, they rallied their strength and pressed forward. Yuan Tan’s army suffered a crushing defeat, and countless common people were killed. Cao Hong charged fiercely through the battle line and came face-to-face with Yuan Tan. Swinging his saber in a flurry of blows, Cao Hong slew him amid the fighting. Seeing the battle line in utter confusion, Guo Tu hurriedly galloped back into the city. Yue Jin spotted him, nocked an arrow to his bow, and shot him down into the moat, where both man and horse fell.

p.src: Cao Cao led his army into Nanpi and reassured the people. Suddenly, a body of troops arrived; they were led by Jiao Chu and Zhang Nan, officers under Yuan Xi. Cao Cao personally led his troops out to meet them. The two generals reversed their weapons, laid down their armor, and came expressly to surrender. Cao Cao enfeoffed them as marquises. Then Zhang Yan, the Black Mountain bandit, came to surrender with an army of one hundred thousand, and Cao Cao appointed him General Who Pacifies the North. He ordered Yuan Tan's head displayed as a warning and decreed that anyone who dared mourn him would be executed. The head was hung outside the northern gate. One man, wearing a cloth cap and mourning clothes, wept beneath the head. Cao Cao's attendants seized him and brought him before Cao Cao. When Cao Cao questioned him, he proved to be Wang Xiu, an Assistant Officer of Qingzhou. He had been expelled for remonstrating with Yuan Tan, but on learning of Tan's death, he had come to mourn him.

p.src: Cao Cao said, “Do you know of my command?” Wang Xiu replied, “I do.” Cao Cao said, “Are you not afraid to die?” Wang Xiu replied, “While he lived, I accepted his summons to office; if I did not mourn him in death, I would be acting against righteousness. If fear of death made me forget righteousness, how could I stand in the world? If I may recover and bury Yuan Tan's body, I shall have no regret even if I am put to death.” Cao Cao said, “How is it that Hebei has so many righteous men! What a pity the Yuan clan could not employ them. Had they been able to do so, how would I ever have dared look this land squarely in the face?” He accordingly ordered Yuan Tan's body recovered and buried, treated Wang Xiu as an honored guest, and appointed him General of the Gentlemen of the Treasury. He then asked him, “Now that Yuan Shang has joined Yuan Xi, what strategy should I use to capture them?” Wang Xiu did not answer. Cao Cao said, “A loyal minister indeed.” He asked Guo Jia, who replied, “Have the Yuan clan's surrendered generals, Jiao Chu, Zhang Nan, and the others attack them.” Cao Cao followed his advice and promptly ordered Jiao Chu, Zhang Nan, Lü Kuang, Lü Xiang, Ma Yan, and Zhang Yi each to lead his own troops and advance against Youzhou by three separate routes. At the same time, he sent Li Dian and Yue Jin to join Zhang Yan, strike Bingzhou, and attack Gao Gan.

p.src: Now Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi, learning that Cao Cao's army was approaching and judging that they could not withstand it, abandoned the city and led their troops away, traveling through the night to Liaoxi, where they sought refuge with the Wuhuan. Wuhuan Chu, Inspector of Youzhou, assembled all the officials of the province, and together they smeared their lips with blood and swore an oath while discussing how to forsake the Yuan clan and submit to Cao Cao. Wuhuan Chu spoke first: “I know that Chancellor Cao is the hero of our age. We shall now go and surrender to him; anyone who disobeys this command will be executed.” They took the blood oath in turn until it came to Assistant Officer Han Heng. Han Heng threw his sword to the ground and cried aloud, “I received profound favor from Lord Yuan and his sons. Now that my lords have been defeated and driven into exile, I lacked the wisdom to save them and the courage to die for them! In this I have already fallen short of righteousness! But to face north and surrender to Cao Cao—I will not do it!”

Lü Kuang and the others led several dozen soldiers straight to the foot of the pass and called out, “We were formerly generals of the Yuan clan and surrendered to Cao Cao only because we had no choice. Cao Cao is treacherous by nature and treats us slightingly, so we have now returned to support our former lord. Open the gate quickly and admit us.” Gao Gan did not believe them at once and merely ordered the two generals to come up into the pass to speak. The two generals removed their armor, abandoned their horses, and entered. They told Gao Gan, “Cao Cao's army has only just arrived. We can take advantage of its unsettled morale and raid its camp tonight. We are willing to lead the attack.”

p.src: Gao Gan was delighted and followed their advice. That night, he ordered the two Lüs to lead the advance with more than ten thousand troops. As they neared Cao Cao's camp, tremendous shouts erupted behind them, and ambush troops rose on every side. Gao Gan realized he had fallen into a trap and hastened back to the city at Huguan. But Yue Jin and Li Dian had already seized the pass. Gao Gan fought his way free and fled to seek refuge with the Chanyu. Cao Cao led his troops to secure the pass and sent men in pursuit of Gao Gan. When Gao Gan reached the Chanyu's territory, he encountered the Wise King of the Left of the northern tribes. Gao Gan dismounted, prostrated himself, and said, “Cao Cao is annexing territory and now intends to invade Your Highness's lands. I earnestly beg you to send aid, so that together we may recover what has been lost and safeguard the north.” The Wise King of the Left said, “I bear Cao Cao no grudge. Why would he invade my lands? Do you wish to make me an enemy of the Cao clan?” He angrily dismissed Gao Gan. Gao Gan considered his plight and, having nowhere else to go, could only seek refuge with Liu Biao. On reaching Shanglu, he was killed by Commandant Wang Yan, who sent his head under guard to Cao Cao. Cao Cao enfeoffed Wang Yan as a marquis.

p.src: Once Bingzhou was pacified, Cao Cao discussed launching a western campaign against the Wuhuan. Cao Hong and the others said, “Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang have lost their armies and generals, and their strength and resources are exhausted. They have fled far into the desert. If we now lead our army west against them, Liu Bei and Liu Biao may take advantage of our absence to raid the capital at Xu. We would be unable to return in time to relieve it, and the resulting disaster would be grave. The best course is to withdraw the army and advance no farther.” Guo Jia said, “What you gentlemen say is mistaken. Though my lord's might shakes the realm, the desert people rely on the remoteness of their frontier and will surely make no preparations. If we take advantage of their unpreparedness and strike them suddenly, we are certain to defeat them. Moreover, Yuan Shao showed favor to the Wuhuan, while the brothers Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi still live; they cannot be left alive. Liu Biao is merely a man of idle talk. He knows his ability is insufficient to control Liu Bei: if he entrusts Bei with great responsibility, he fears he will be unable to restrain him; if he gives him only minor duties, Bei will not serve him. Though you empty the state to campaign afar, my lord need have no concern.” Cao Cao said, “Fengxiao's words are entirely correct.”

p.src: He then led all three divisions of his army, great and small, with several thousand wagons, and advanced onward. They saw only boundless yellow sands, while fierce winds rose on every side. The roads were rugged, and men and horses found the going difficult. Cao Cao began to consider withdrawing and asked Guo Jia's advice. At this time, Guo Jia had fallen ill from the unfamiliar climate and lay sick in his carriage. Cao Cao wept and said, “Because I wished to pacify the desert, I made you endure the hardships of this long journey, until you fell ill. How can my heart be at peace?” Guo Jia said, “I am deeply grateful for Your Excellency's great kindness. Even if I died, I could not repay one ten-thousandth of it.” Cao Cao said, “Seeing how rugged the northern country is, I am minded to withdraw. What do you think?” Guo Jia said, “In war, speed is paramount. Now that we are striking an enemy a thousand li away, our heavy baggage is too great for us to seize the advantage. Better to take light troops and advance swiftly by forced marches, falling upon the enemy unprepared. We need only find someone who knows the roads to serve as our guide.”

p.src: Cao Cao accordingly left Guo Jia in Yizhou to recover and sought a local guide to lead the way. Someone recommended Tian Chou, a former general under Yuan Shao, saying that he knew the region well, so Cao Cao summoned and questioned him. Tian Chou said, “During summer and autumn, this road is flooded. Where the water is shallow, carts and horses cannot pass; where it is deep, it cannot bear boats. Movement is extremely difficult. It would be better to turn back, pass through the mouth of Lulong, cross the perilous ground at Baitan, and emerge into the undefended country. From there, Liucheng lies near ahead. By falling upon the enemy unprepared, we may capture Maodun in a single battle.”

p.src: Cao Cao followed his advice, appointed Tian Chou General Who Pacifies the North, and made him the local guide at the head of the vanguard. Zhang Liao came next. Cao Cao himself brought up the rear, advancing with light cavalry at double speed. Tian Chou led Zhang Liao forward to White Wolf Mountain, where they encountered Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang advancing with Maodun and tens of thousands of cavalry. Zhang Liao galloped back to report to Cao Cao. Cao Cao reined in his horse, climbed to high ground, and looked out. He saw that Maodun's troops had no proper formations and stood in disorderly ranks. Cao Cao said to Zhang Liao, “The enemy ranks are in disorder; we can attack them at once.” He then handed his command standard to Zhang Liao. Zhang Liao led Xu Chu, Yu Jin, and Xu Huang down the mountain by four separate routes, launching a fierce and rapid assault. Maodun's army fell into utter confusion. Zhang Liao spurred his horse forward and cut Maodun down from the saddle; all the remaining troops surrendered. Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang led several thousand cavalrymen away to seek refuge in Liaodong.

p.src: Cao Cao withdrew his army into Liucheng and enfeoffed Tian Chou as Marquis of Liuting, charging him with the defense of Liucheng. Tian Chou wept and said, “I am merely a man who forsook his duty and fled. Through your great kindness I have been spared and kept alive, which is already more good fortune than I deserve. How could I sell the stronghold at Lulong in exchange for rewards and emoluments? Even at the cost of my life, I dare not accept a marquisate.” Admiring his righteousness, Cao Cao appointed Tian Chou a Court Gentleman for Consultation instead. Cao Cao consoled and reassured the Chanyu’s people, acquired ten thousand fine horses, and began the return march that very day. The weather was then bitterly cold and dry. For two hundred li there was no water, and the army was also short of provisions, so horses were slaughtered for food. Only after digging thirty or forty feet into the earth did they find water. On returning to Yizhou, Cao Cao richly rewarded those who had previously advised against the expedition. He then said to his generals, “Previously, I took advantage of a perilous situation to conduct a distant campaign and succeeded only by good fortune. Though we were victorious, it was Heaven that favored us; this must not be taken as a precedent. Your counsel was the surest and safest course, and therefore I reward you. In future, never hesitate to speak your minds.”

p.src: By the time Cao Cao reached Yizhou, Guo Jia had been dead for several days, and his coffin rested in the government offices. Cao Cao went to offer sacrifice and wept bitterly, saying, “Fengxiao’s death is Heaven’s ruin of me!” Turning to the assembled officials, he said, “All of you are about my own age; only Fengxiao was younger. I meant to entrust him with affairs after my death, but never expected him to perish in the prime of life. My heart is torn apart!” Guo Jia’s attendants presented a sealed letter he had written as he lay dying and said, “Lord Guo wrote this with his own hand before his death and instructed us: ‘If the Chancellor follows what is written here, the affair in Liaodong will be settled.’” Cao Cao opened the letter and read it, nodding and sighing. None of those present understood what it meant.

p.src: The next day, Xiahou Dun led the others in to report: “Gongsun Kang, Administrator of Liaodong, has long refused submission. Now Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang have gone to seek refuge with him, and they are certain to become a future menace. We should march swiftly against them before they make a move; then Liaodong can be taken.” Cao Cao laughed. “There is no need to trouble you gentlemen to display your martial might. Within a few days, Gongsun Kang will deliver the heads of the two Yuans himself.” None of the generals believed him.

p.src: Now Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang, leading several thousand horsemen, fled toward Liaodong. Gongsun Kang, Administrator of Liaodong, was a native of Xiangping and the son of Gongsun Du, General of Martial Might. When he learned that day that Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang were coming to seek refuge, he gathered his subordinate officials to discuss the matter. Gongsun Gong said, “While Yuan Shao lived, he always harbored designs on Liaodong. Now Yuan Xi and Yuan Shang, defeated and facing destruction, have nowhere to shelter and come seeking refuge here. Their purpose is that of a cuckoo usurping a magpie’s nest. If we take them in, they will surely plot against us later. Better to lure them into the city, kill them, and present their heads to Lord Cao. He will certainly treat us generously.” Gongsun Kang said, “I fear only that Cao Cao may lead his army down into Liaodong. Perhaps it would be better to receive the two Yuans and use them as our allies.” Gongsun Gong replied, “We can send someone to gather intelligence. If Cao Cao’s forces come to attack, we shall keep the two Yuans. If he makes no move, we shall kill them and send them to Lord Cao.” Gongsun Kang agreed and sent men to learn the news.

For now we shall seek refuge with Gongsun Kang; later we will kill him and seize his territory. Once we have restored our strength and can oppose the Central Plains, we may recover Hebei.”

p.src: Their plan settled, they went to see Gongsun Kang. He lodged them at the posthouse but pleaded illness and did not receive them at once. Before many days had passed, a spy returned and reported, “Cao Cao’s army remains encamped at Yizhou and shows no intention of advancing into Liaodong.” Gongsun Kang was delighted. He first concealed armed executioners behind the wall hangings, then summoned the two Yuans inside. After they had exchanged formal greetings, he ordered them to sit. The weather was bitterly cold. Seeing no mat or cushion on the couch, Yuan Shang said to Gongsun Kang, “I should like a mat laid down for me.” Gongsun Kang glared at him and said, “The heads of you two are about to travel ten thousand li! What need have you of a mat?” Yuan Shang was horrified. Gongsun Kang shouted, “Why have you men not struck yet?” The executioners rushed out and beheaded both men there upon the sitting mat. Their heads were placed in wooden boxes and sent to Yizhou to be presented to Cao Cao.
